title: Asian Stocks Plunge Amid Growing Doubts Over AI Boom Surge
body:
Asian equity markets tumbled on Tuesday, with the region’s tech‑heavy indices posting some of their steepest declines in months as investors grew increasingly skeptical about the sustainability of the artificial‑intelligence rally that has buoyed stocks since the start of the year. The sell‑off was led by South Korea’s KOSPI, which slumped more than 2 % in early trading, while Japan’s Nikkei, Taiwan’s TAIEX and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng each fell between 1.5 % and 2 %, erasing gains accumulated over the past week.

The downturn follows a rapid reversal of the optimism that surged after Nvidia’s co‑founder Jensen Huang reassumed the chief‑executive role in early February, a move that had initially sparked a wave of buying across semiconductor and AI‑related firms. Analysts now warn that the sector’s exuberance may have outpaced the underlying fundamentals, pointing to a combination of lofty profit expectations, tightening monetary policy and lingering supply‑chain constraints that could dampen demand for AI‑driven hardware and services.

In South Korea, the market’s sharp slide was amplified by heavy weighting in memory‑chip manufacturers such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, whose shares have been volatile after recent earnings reports hinted at weaker-than‑expected demand from data‑center operators. The broader KOSPI also felt pressure from the country’s financial sector, where rising yields on government bonds have prompted a shift away from risk‑ier equities. Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei was dragged down by a slump in domestic chipmakers and a modest decline in export‑oriented manufacturers, reflecting concerns that global customers may postpone capital‑intensive AI projects amid uncertain economic outlooks.

Taiwan’s market, heavily reliant on the world’s leading foundry, TSMC, experienced a pullback after the company warned of a potential slowdown in AI‑related orders in the second quarter. The warning came despite TSMC’s record‑breaking capacity expansions, underscoring the delicate balance between supply‑side ambition and demand‑side reality. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng’s decline was broader, with both technology and property stocks falling as investors reassessed valuation levels after a period of rapid price appreciation driven by mainland capital flows.

Market commentators suggest that the current correction may be a necessary recalibration rather than a sign of a prolonged downturn. “The AI narrative has been a powerful catalyst, but it is now being tested against real‑world adoption curves and macro‑economic headwinds,” said a senior strategist at a regional brokerage. “We are likely to see a more measured pace of investment, with investors focusing on companies that can demonstrate sustainable revenue streams rather than speculative hype.”

Looking ahead, the trajectory of Asian tech stocks will hinge on several key factors. First, the release of quarterly earnings from major AI hardware producers will provide clearer guidance on demand trends. Second, central banks in the region are expected to continue tightening monetary policy, which could further pressure equity valuations if rate hikes persist. Finally, the pace at which enterprises integrate generative‑AI tools into core operations will determine whether the sector can maintain its growth momentum.

If the AI boom proves resilient, the correction could set the stage for a healthier, earnings‑driven rally later in the year. Conversely, a prolonged slowdown in AI spending would likely keep sentiment subdued, prompting investors to rotate toward more defensive assets. For now, market participants appear poised to watch closely how the interplay of corporate performance, monetary policy and real‑world AI adoption shapes the next chapter for Asian equities.
